mainTopic: Explaining the dispute over the fourth wife's oath, one partner going to court for another, and two deeds dated the same day
overview: The משנה taught about a man who married four wives and died. The תנא קמא says the fourth wife collects her כתובה without swearing to the earlier wives, and בן ננס says she must swear. The גמרא gives three explanations of this dispute. The first is about whether a later creditor who collected first keeps what he took. The second, from רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה, is about whether we worry that she will wear down the field. The third, from אביי, is about whether אביי קשישא's rule protects adult orphans with an oath. Next, רב הונא rules that when one of two brothers or partners goes to court, he acts as the other's agent. רב נחמן tries to prove this from the four wives' oaths, but the גמרא rejects the proof: the absent partner can say he would have argued better, though only if he was out of town. Finally, רב and שמואל argue about two deeds dated the same day. The גמרא begins asking whether רב follows רבי מאיר's view that the signing witnesses make a deed take effect, and that question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The case: a field turns out not to belong to the husband
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets up the exact case behind the dispute of the תנא קמא and בן ננס. One field of the estate turns out not to be the husband's, and the two sides argue about a later creditor who collected first.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where one of the fields turns out not to be his. They are arguing about a later creditor who went ahead and collected first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is explaining what the dispute in the משנה is really about. It describes the case and names the general rule they argue over, setting up the two opinions that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a field given to an earlier wife is taken away because it was never the husband's, that wife ends up with nothing. Can she then take back what the fourth wife already collected? That is the same as asking whether a creditor with a later-dated loan, who collected first, must give it up to the earlier creditor.

keyTerms.meaning: A field that does not belong to him; it may be taken away by its real owner
A later creditor, whose loan document has a later date
He went first and collected
They disagree about

steps.confusionAlert: The fourth wife is compared to the 'later creditor'. Her כתובה was written last, yet she might be the one who ends up holding property while an earlier wife is left with nothing.

phrases.english: Such as where one of them was found to be
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the fields left in the husband's estate.

phrases.english: a field that is not his.
And regarding a later creditor
who went first and collected, they disagree.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּגוֹן שֶׁנִּמְצֵאת אַחַת מֵהֶן שָׂדֶה שֶׁאֵינָהּ שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the גמרא's answer to what the תנא קמא and בן ננס are arguing about in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the basis of the dispute between the תנא קמא and בן ננס about the fourth wife's oath?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case is where one field turns out not to be the husband's, and they argue about a later creditor who collected first.

steps.title: The first opinion: what he collected can be taken back
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא holds that a later creditor who collected first does not get to keep it. The earlier creditor can take it from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא קמא holds: what he collected, he did not really collect.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the view of the תנא קמא. A later creditor who collected first must give the property up to the earlier creditor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Applied to the wives: if an earlier wife loses her field, she can take what the fourth wife collected. So the fourth wife does not need to swear to the earlier wives, because anything she collects can be taken from her anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed opinion in the משנה
What he collected is not really his; it can be taken back

phrases.english: The first tanna holds:
What he collected, he did not collect.
phrases.notes: He means the earlier creditor can still take it away from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first side of the dispute set up in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A later creditor who collected first must give it up to the earlier creditor, so the fourth wife needs no oath.

steps.title: בן ננס: what he collected he keeps
steps.stepSummary: בן ננס holds that a later creditor who collected first keeps what he took. That is why the fourth wife must swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: And בן ננס holds: what he collected, he collected.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives בן ננס's side. Once the later creditor collects, the property is his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Applied to the wives: what the fourth wife collects cannot be taken back by the earlier wives. Because she keeps it for good, she must swear that she is collecting properly, so the earlier wives are not hurt.

keyTerms.meaning: What he collected stays his

steps.whatToRemember: First explanation: the dispute depends on whether a later creditor who collected first keeps it. The תנא קמא says no, so no oath is needed. בן ננס says yes, so an oath is needed.

phrases.english: And ben Nanas holds:
What he collected, he collected.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing side to the תנא קמא's view in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A later creditor who collected first keeps it, so the fourth wife must swear before collecting.

steps.title: A different explanation: worry that she will damage the field
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן, quoting רבה בר אבוה, says everyone agrees that the later creditor's collection can be taken back. The real dispute is whether we worry she will ruin the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: Everyone agrees that what he collected, he did not really collect. Here they argue about whether we worry that she will damage the field.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא offers a different way to explain the dispute in the משנה. He removes the first explanation's argument and puts a new one in its place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבה בר אבוה, both sides agree with the תנא קמא's rule from step 2: the earlier wife can take the field back. Still, while the fourth wife holds it she might lower its value. The question is only whether that worry is enough to require an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
We are concerned / we worry
She will make it lose value (ruin or wear down the field)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two explanations. In this one, nobody holds 'what he collected he keeps'. The argument has moved to a completely different issue.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the משנה's dispute can be explained without anyone holding that a later creditor keeps what he collected first.

phrases.aramaic: (אָמַר) רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Rabba bar Avuh said:
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. Either way, רב נחמן is quoting רבה בר אבוה.

phrases.english: Everyone agrees:
what he collected, he did not collect.
And here, about whether we are concerned
that perhaps she will damage it, they disagree,
phrases.notes: Literally 'make it pale'. The worry is that she will wear down the field so it is worth less when it is taken back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the explanation in steps 1-3 with a different explanation of the same dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everyone agrees that a later creditor who collected first must give it up. The dispute is whether we worry she will lower the field's value.

steps.title: The two sides of the worry that she will ruin the field
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן's explanation is spelled out. One side worries she will ruin the field and the other side does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage (בן ננס) holds that we worry she might ruin the field. The other Sage (the תנא קמא) holds that we do not worry about that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב נחמן's explanation from Step 4. It tells us which side worries that she will ruin the field and which side does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בן ננס is afraid that a wife who knows she might lose the field later will drain it now and never take care of it. So he makes her swear, so that she feels her hold on the field is secure and treats it well. The תנא קמא does not have this worry, so he sees no reason for an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: We are concerned / we worry about
She will ruin (drain) the field
One Sage holds

phrases.english: One Sage holds: we are concerned that perhaps she will ruin [the field].

phrases.aramaic: וּמַר סָבַר: לָא חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא תַּכְסִיף.
phrases.english: And one Sage holds: we are not concerned that perhaps she will ruin [the field].
phrases.notes: This is the תנא קמא, so he does not require her to swear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב נחמן's statement by assigning each side of the worry to one of the תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בן ננס worries that she will ruin the field, so he requires an oath. The תנא קמא has no such worry.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב נחמן, both sides agree that a later creditor's collection can be taken back. Their only disagreement is whether we worry that she will ruin the field.

steps.title: אביי says the dispute depends on אביי קשישא's rule about orphans
steps.stepSummary: אביי gives a different explanation of the dispute. It depends on אביי קשישא's teaching that even adult orphans are protected by the oath requirement.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The difference between them is the ruling of אביי קשישא. אביי קשישא taught: The orphans the Sages spoke about, from whom no one can collect without an oath, include adults, and of course minors.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers a different reason why the תנא קמא and בן ננס disagree. He brings a teaching of אביי קשישא, and the next step will apply it to the dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually anyone who collects from orphans must swear first, because the orphans do not know their father's business. אביי קשישא says this applies even to adult orphans. The fourth wife collects from the husband's estate, which now belongs to his heirs, so this rule could explain why she must swear.

keyTerms.meaning: אביי the Elder, an earlier sage, different from the famous אביי
There is [a difference] between them
Orphans (the heirs, from whom collection requires an oath)
And needless to say

phrases.english: Abaye said:
The [ruling] of Abaye the Elder is [the difference] between them.
phrases.notes: אביי the Elder is a different, earlier sage, not the famous אביי who is speaking here.

phrases.english: As Abaye the Elder taught:
The orphans that [the Sages] spoke of include adults,
phrases.notes: He means the rule that nobody can collect from orphans without swearing first.

phrases.english: and needless to say, minors.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי אָמַר: דְּאַבָּיֵי קַשִּׁישָׁא אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different explanation of the dispute in place of רב נחמן's concern about ruining the field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The oath required to collect from orphans applies even when the orphans are adults.

steps.title: Who accepts אביי קשישא's rule
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא does not accept אביי קשישא's rule, so the wife does not swear. בן ננס accepts it, so she must swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא קמא does not hold like אביי קשישא. בן ננס does hold like אביי קשישא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies אביי קשישא's rule to the two sides of the dispute and finishes אביי's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the orphans are adults. According to the תנא קמא, the oath only protects minor orphans, so the fourth wife can collect from adults without swearing. בן ננס protects even adult orphans, so she must swear before she collects.

keyTerms.meaning: The first (unnamed) Sage in the משנה
He does not hold [this rule]
He holds [this rule]

phrases.aramaic: תַּנָּא קַמָּא לֵית לֵיהּ דְּאַבָּיֵי קַשִּׁישָׁא.
phrases.english: The first Tanna does not hold [the ruling] of Abaye the Elder.

phrases.aramaic: וּבֶן נַנָּס אִית לֵיהּ דְּאַבָּיֵי קַשִּׁישָׁא.
phrases.english: And ben Nanas holds [the ruling] of Abaye the Elder.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּא קַמָּא לֵית לֵיהּ דְּאַבָּיֵי קַשִּׁישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the teaching quoted in Step 6 to the two sides of the dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תנא קמא rejects אביי קשישא's rule, so there is no oath. בן ננס accepts it, so there is an oath.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two explanations of the dispute. רב נחמן says it is about whether she will ruin the field. אביי says it is about whether adult orphans are protected by an oath.

steps.title: One brother or partner in court acts as agent for the other
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that if one of two brothers or partners goes to court against a third person, the other one is bound by the result.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: Two brothers or two partners have a court case against one person, and one of them went to court with him. The other one cannot say to that person, 'You are not my opponent in court.' The one who went to court acted as his agent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. רב הונא gives a rule about brothers or partners who share a court case against one person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose one partner goes to court and loses. The other partner cannot ask for a new trial by saying he was never part of the case. The one who went counts as his agent, so the ruling binds both of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Partners
The opposing party in a court case
He acted as his agent
He cannot [claim]

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
These two brothers or two partners
who have a court case against one [person],
and one of them went to court with him,
the other cannot say to him:

phrases.aramaic: אַתְּ לָאו בַּעַל דְּבָרִים דִּידִי אַתְּ.
phrases.english: You are not my opponent in court.
Rather, he acted as his agent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: הָנֵי תְּרֵי אַחֵי וּתְרֵי שׁוּתָּפֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the fourth wife's oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When one brother or partner goes to court, he is treated as the other's agent, so the ruling binds both of them.
steps.whyThisMatters: It means one court case can settle a shared claim, so the other side does not have to win the same case twice.

steps.title: The people of סורא ask רב נחמן about the brothers' case
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן comes to סורא, and the people there ask him the law in a case like רב הונא's, where only one brother or partner went to court.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן once came to סורא. They asked him: what is the law in a case like this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story to set up the next move. People ask רב נחמן what the law is when only one of two brothers or partners went to court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'A case like this' points back to רב הונא's case in Step 8. The question is whether the brother or partner who was not there must accept the result of a case he did not argue himself. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Happened to come, visited
סורא, a major city of Torah learning in Babylonia
In a case like this
They asked him

phrases.english: Rav Nachman happened to come to Sura.
They asked him: In a case like this, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the law in the case that רב הונא ruled on in Step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the absent brother or partner bound by the court result that the other one received?

steps.title: רב נחמן's proof from the משנה of the four wives
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers from the משנה: the first wife swears only to the second wife, not to the third. This shows that the second wife acted as the third wife's agent, so one person's claim counts for another.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: It is a משנה. 'The first wife swears to the second, the second to the third, and the third to the fourth.' But the משנה does not say that the first wife swears to the third. What is the reason? Isn't it because the second wife already did the third wife's job as her agent?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers the question with a proof from a משנה. He wants to show that what one person does in court counts for another person with the same interest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The third wife also has reason to want the first wife to swear, yet the משנה never makes the first wife swear to her. רב נחמן explains that when the second wife demanded the oath, she was acting for the third wife too. In the same way, one brother in court acts for the other, which supports רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a משנה, meaning the answer is already taught in a משנה
Swears, takes an oath
It does not teach, it is not mentioned
She did her job as an agent, she acted on her behalf

steps.whyThisMatters: רב נחמן is trying to show the idea behind רב הונא's ruling: a person with the same interest can stand in for you in court. The next step pushes this proof away.

phrases.english: He said to them: It is a Mishnah:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in our פרק about a man who married four wives and died.

phrases.english: The first wife swears to the second,
and the second to the third, and the third to the fourth.
But that the first swears to the third, it does not teach.
What is the reason?
Is it not because she (the second) did her (the third's) agency?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 9 with a proof from a משנה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The absent brother or partner is bound, just as the third wife is covered by the oath the second wife demanded.
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's rule that one partner's court case binds the other.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of the four wives, which lists no oath from the first wife to the third.

steps.title: The proof is rejected: an oath is not like a court argument
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. An oath is the same no matter who demands it, but a partner in a court case can say he would have argued better.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are the cases really alike? There, an oath to one person is the same as an oath to a hundred. Here, the other partner can say: 'If I had been there, I would have argued better.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off רב נחמן's proof by showing that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the third wife loses nothing, because the first wife's oath would be exactly the same if she demanded it herself. In a lawsuit, though, the way a case is argued can change the result. So the absent partner has a real complaint, and the משנה does not prove רב הונא's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it comparable? This phrase is used to reject a comparison
An oath to one is like an oath to a hundred, meaning one oath covers everyone
I would have argued more, or argued better

steps.confusionAlert: This step does more than knock down the proof. Its reasoning, 'had I been there, I would have argued better,' gives the absent partner a real objection to רב הונא's rule. The next step limits that objection to a partner who was out of town, so רב הונא's rule still holds when he was in town.

phrases.english: Is it comparable?
There, an oath to one is an oath to a hundred,

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא אָמַר: אִילּוּ אֲנָא הֲוַאי, טָעֵינְנָא טְפֵי.
phrases.english: Here, he can say: Had I been there, I would have argued better.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the משנה of the four wives. Its reasoning also gives the absent partner a claim against being bound, which step 12 limits to when he was out of town.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: An oath comes out the same whoever demands it, but a court argument depends on who presents it.

steps.title: The absent partner's claim works only if he was out of town
steps.stepSummary: The claim 'I would have argued better' only works if the partner was out of town. If he was in town, he should have come to court, so he is bound by the result.
steps.simpleTranslation: We said this only when he was not in town. But if he was in town, he should have come.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits when the absent partner can say 'I would have argued better.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the partner could easily have come to court and chose not to, he showed that he was relying on his brother or partner. So in that case he cannot complain, and רב הונא's ruling applies.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when, which introduces a limit on a rule
He is in town
He should have come

steps.whatToRemember: If one brother or partner goes to court, the other is bound by the result if he was in town and did not come. If he was out of town, he can say 'I would have argued better.'

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא אִיתֵיהּ בְּמָתָא,
phrases.english: And we said this only when he is not in town,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the absent partner's claim that he would have argued better.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אִיתֵיהּ בְּמָתָא — אִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְמֵיתֵי.
phrases.english: but if he is in town, he should have come.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the claim from Step 11 so that it applies only when the partner was away.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An absent partner who was in town is bound by the court result. Only one who was out of town can say he would have argued better.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב הונא's ruling applies when the other partner was in town and chose not to come.

steps.title: Two deeds with the same date: split it, or let the judges decide
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל disagree about two deeds for one property that are dated the same day. רב says the holders divide it. שמואל says it goes by שודא דדייני, the judges' judgment.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: if two deeds for the same property both carry the same date, רב said the two holders split it, and שמואל said the judges decide by their own judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new argument between רב and שמואל. The case is two deeds for the same property that are both dated the same day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Deeds usually show only the day, not the hour, so we cannot tell which one came first. רב treats the two holders as equal and has them share the property. שמואל gives the judges the power to decide which holder should get it.

keyTerms.meaning: Legal documents, such as a deed of sale or a deed of gift.
"That come out on one day," meaning both deeds carry the same date.
They divide or split the property between them.
The judges' own judgment. The judges decide who gets the property.

steps.confusionAlert: שודא דדייני does not mean the judges split the property. It means the judges pick which holder gets it, based on their own sense of the case.
steps.whyThisMatters: This argument becomes the base for the rest of the discussion, where the גמרא looks for the reason behind each opinion.

phrases.aramaic: אִתְּמַר: שְׁנֵי שְׁטָרוֹת הַיּוֹצְאִים בְּיוֹם אֶחָד,
phrases.english: It was stated: two deeds that come out on one day,
phrases.notes: Picture one person giving or selling the same field to two different people, with both deeds dated the same day.

phrases.english: Rav said: they divide it,
and Shmuel said: it is up to the judges' judgment.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִתְּמַר: שְׁנֵי שְׁטָרוֹת הַיּוֹצְאִים בְּיוֹם אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, separate from the earlier discussion about partners going to court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two deeds with the same date: according to רב the holders split the property. According to שמואל it is decided by שודא דדייני.

steps.title: Is רב following רבי מאיר about the signing witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רב's ruling to split the property is based on רבי מאיר's view that עדי חתימה, the signing witnesses, are what make a deed take effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should we say that רב holds like רבי מאיר, who said that the witnesses who sign the deed are what make it work?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes a source for רב's opinion. This line sets up the next move, where the גמרא will test whether this link is correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds that a deed works because of the witnesses who signed it. If so, both deeds became valid on the same signed date, and neither is stronger than the other. That would explain why רב has the two holders split it.

keyTerms.meaning: "Shall we say?" The גמרא suggests a link or a source, and that suggestion is often rejected later.
